source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: Dynamic benchmark of 1,000 auto-generated questions that are unresolved at submission, so no leakage. Experts beat the best LLM.
numbers: Human comparison on a random 200-question subset. Superforecasters (39) Brier 0.096; public 0.121; best LLM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, with crowd forecast as input) 0.122; p<0.001 vs superforecasters.
quote: Expert forecasters outperform the top-performing LLM (p-value < 0.001).
limits: Top LLMs had the market crowd forecast as input. Humans surveyed once (mid-2024).
agent_relevance: Direct anchor: this is the gap our agent must close.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: Without the crowd forecast as input, LLMs are clearly worse.
numbers: Best LLM without crowd forecast on market questions: Brier 0.136, vs 0.122 with it. Random 50% baseline is 0.25.
limits: Freeze values leak human skill, so 0.122 is not pure model skill.
agent_relevance: Do not count a pasted market price as reasoning; report with and without anchors.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: News retrieval did not help LLMs on ForecastBench.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet scratchpad with crowd value 0.128 vs scratchpad with news and crowd value 0.132 (leaderboard tables). Paper text: access to recent news did not improve performance.
limits: Retrieval was the Halawi et al. pipeline. Later work (AIA, Bridgewater) shows better agentic search does help.
agent_relevance: Naive retrieval is not a free win; search quality matters.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: LLMs do badly on combination questions (joint events); the gap widens.
numbers: Superforecasters 0.076, public 0.096, top LLM (GPT-4o) 0.130 on the set with combination questions. Gap 0.054 vs 0.026 between GPT-4o and GPT-4.
limits: Human combination forecasts were built assuming independence, a lower bound on human skill.
agent_relevance: Joint-probability coherence is a weak spot; test it in our scaffold.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: Forecast accuracy tracks general model strength; linear extrapolation gives a parity point.
numbers: Brier vs Chatbot Arena r=-0.68, p=0.003, fit y=0.506-0.000298x, R2=0.47, parity near Arena 1406 (95% CI 1346-1633). Vs log training compute r=-0.67, p=0.046, parity at 6.49e26 FLOP (CI 9.69e25 to 8.65e28).
limits: About 16 models; wide CI; linear trend assumed.
agent_relevance: Raw model gains may beat scaffold gains unless the scaffold adds calibration.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench
finding: Simple LLM ensembles (3 models x 3 prompts) are modest and still short of humans.
numbers: Appendix: median aggregate 0.197, geometric mean of log odds 0.194. Single models 0.178 (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) to 0.282 (Llama-2-70B) on that table.
limits: Appendix subset and scoring base differ from Table 2.
agent_relevance: Aggregating diverse samples helps but does not close the gap alone.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Retrieval-augmented, fine-tuned GPT-4 system approaches the human crowd on questions after the model cutoff.
numbers: Test set 914 questions (from Jun 2023). System Brier 0.179 vs best base model 0.208 (GPT-4-1106) vs crowd 0.149; random 0.250. Accuracy 71.5% vs crowd 77.0%.
quote: On average, the system nears the crowd aggregate of competitive forecasters, and in some settings surpasses it.
limits: Still worse than the crowd on average. Crowd is a many-forecaster aggregate, not superforecasters.
agent_relevance: Pipeline (queries, filter, summarise, several reasoners, trimmed mean) is a template for our states.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: System beats the crowd only in a selective setting; loses when the crowd is confident.
numbers: Crowd uncertain (0.3-0.7): system 0.199 vs crowd 0.246. Beats crowd by more than 1.5 SE when uncertain crowd, early retrieval dates and 5+ articles all hold. 5+ articles alone: 0.238 vs 0.240.
limits: Criteria chosen post hoc. System rarely outputs low probabilities (safety hedging).
agent_relevance: Add an anti-hedging, extremizing step when evidence is strong.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Blending the system with the crowd beats either alone.
numbers: Aggregate of system plus crowd outperformed both alone (Section 6.4). Trimmed mean was best of 5 ensemble rules on validation.
limits: Needs a crowd forecast at question time.
agent_relevance: Use an outside prior as a blended input, not a replacement.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Ablation: fine-tuned reasoner and retrieval both contribute.
numbers: Dropping the fine-tuned reasoner worsened Brier; dropping retrieval too worsened it further (Table 5 rows 5-6).
limits: Fine-tuning used outputs that beat the crowd on training questions; gains not separated by size here.
agent_relevance: Reasoning traces that beat a reference are a useful signal for exemplars.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Median of 12 LLMs matches a human tournament crowd on 31 binary questions.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs 0.25 no-information, t(30)=-2.35, p=0.026. Vs 925 humans: no difference (p=0.850). Equivalence at bound 0.081 Brier: p=0.017 and p=0.040.
limits: Only 31 questions; wide bounds; equivalence test not preregistered.
agent_relevance: Wisdom of crowds works for LLM samples: aggregate several draws.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: LLMs show acquiescence bias: predictions skew above 50%.
numbers: Median forecast 60%, mean 57.35 (SD 20.93), t(1006)=86.20, p<0.001, yet only 14 of 31 questions resolved yes. Median aggregation reduced the bias.
limits: Near-even outcome split; bias size may differ on rare-event sets.
agent_relevance: Guard against yes-bias with a base-rate check.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Study 2: showing the median human forecast to GPT-4 or Claude 2 helps, but plain averaging helps more.
numbers: Accuracy improved 17% to 28% with the human median as information; simple human-machine average was more accurate than the updated model forecasts.
limits: Models may anchor rather than reason.
agent_relevance: Averaging an agent forecast with an outside prior can beat letting the agent adjust it.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) AI-Augmented Predictions
finding: An LLM assistant raised human forecasting accuracy, even a noisy overconfident one.
numbers: N=991 analysed (1,152 recruited, Prolific). Both assistants +24% to +28% accuracy vs control; without one outlier item +41% (superforecasting) vs +29% (noisy).
limits: Outlier item drove results; control had a weaker model; no consistent extra benefit for low-skill forecasters.
agent_relevance: Numeric advice helps humans even when biased; report outlier sensitivity.

source: Zou et al. (2022) Forecasting Future World Events with Neural Networks (Autocast)
finding: Autocast: first tournament-question benchmark with dated news; models far below humans.
numbers: Best model 65% accuracy true/false vs 92% human crowd (50% random). Scores rise with model size (0.2B to 2.8B) and with news retrieval.
limits: 2022 retrieval-augmented T5/FiD, not instruction-tuned LLMs.
agent_relevance: Baseline for speed of progress: 27-point accuracy gap in 2022 to a Brier gap near 0.03 by 2024-25.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: Many backtested LLM-forecasting wins are suspect due to leakage.
numbers: At least 3.8% of Halawi et al. questions resolved early; at least 10% of Tao et al. (2025) trivial; weak classifiers reach over 80% accuracy on Dai et al. (2025) news-generated binary questions; over 90% of that set judged over-specific.
limits: The 90% figure is the authors' subjective estimate.
agent_relevance: Use unresolved or hermetic questions; check for logical leakage.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: Date-filtered search leaks the future, and retrieval models are trained on future data.
numbers: Figures show date-restricted searches returning later-dated content. Resolution error 1-5% reported when resolving with Perplexity-based retrieval.
limits: Examples, not a measured rate.
agent_relevance: Do not trust retrieval gains measured on resolved questions.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: Brier scores are not comparable across base rates.
numbers: Example: 50 coin-flip + 50 rare (5%) questions. Perfect on rare events gives total about 0.125. Improving coin-flip from 0.25 to 0.15 gives about 0.10 and looks better.
limits: Illustrative arithmetic.
agent_relevance: Report per-stratum and base-rate-relative scores.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Logical-consistency violations predict real Brier score, allowing instant evaluation.
numbers: Correlation with Brier up to 0.92 (conditional arbitrage check), 0.85 (frequentist average violation), 0.49 (an arbitrage aggregate). Some checks carry little signal.
limits: Few forecasters; correlation not causation.
agent_relevance: Cheap self-check: ask coherence checks (P(A), P(not A), conditionals) in the schema.

source: Turtel et al. (2025) Outcome-based Reinforcement Learning to Predict the Future
finding: RL on resolved market outcomes lifts a 14B model to o1 level and improves calibration.
numbers: 1,265-question holdout. ReMax 7-run ensemble Brier 0.190 (CI 0.178-0.203), ECE 0.062; o1 0.202, ECE 0.093. Market about 0.039 better (0.151). Polymarket sim profit $52 vs $39 for o1.
limits: Still worse than the market price; one platform; noisy rewards.
agent_relevance: Calibration is learnable; a scaffold can imitate it by recalibration.

source: FutureSearch (2025) Bench to the Future
finding: Pastcasting (resolved questions with frozen offline web) tracks progress across model generations.
numbers: Weighted Brier: Sonnet 3.5 orig 0.1925; 3.5 v2 0.1690; 3.7 0.1712; 3.7 thinking 0.1645; Sonnet 4 0.1560; 4 thinking 0.1597; Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.1611. 3.5 orig vs Sonnet 4 p=0.0024.
limits: Thinking gave no clear gain (Sonnet 4 vs 4 thinking p=0.53). No human baseline. About 178.8 effective questions.
agent_relevance: Extended thinking alone did not buy accuracy; structure and calibration matter.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster Technical Report
finding: Agentic forecaster with supervisor and Platt scaling is statistically level with superforecasters on ForecastBench.
numbers: FB-7-21 (498 q): AIA 0.1076, superforecasters 0.1110, public 0.1451, o3 0.133. FB-8-14 (602 q): superforecasters 0.1152, public 0.1510, prior best LLM 0.145. FB-Market: AIA 0.0753 vs superforecasters 0.0740 vs market 0.0965.
quote: statistically indistinguishable from superforecasters on ForecastBench
limits: Industry report, not peer reviewed; market prices as input on market subset; on harder MarketLiquid (1,610 q) AIA 0.1258 loses to market 0.1106 though the ensemble beats the market.
agent_relevance: Closest evidence that a scaffold can reach superforecaster level; copy agentic search, supervisor, extremizing.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster Technical Report
finding: Search quality matters: agentic beats non-agentic; weak search equals no search.
numbers: No search 0.1230; Search-B non-agentic 0.12168; Search-B agentic 0.11824; Search-A non-agentic 0.11738; Search-A agentic 0.1140.
limits: Providers anonymised; effect shrinks once market prices are given.
agent_relevance: Explains why Karger found no news gain; use iterative query strategy.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster Technical Report
finding: Market price as input gives about 11-12% gain and reduces the value of search.
numbers: No-news 0.116 to 0.103 with market price (11.2%). Best config 0.085 to 0.075 (11.8%), market-derived ForecastBench subset.
limits: Only market questions.
agent_relevance: Anchor on a strong prior, then update.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster Technical Report
finding: Platt scaling (equal to log-odds extremization) fixes LLM hedging; prompt tweaks did not.
numbers: Platt scaling on the mean of k forecasts gave the lowest Brier; coefficient sqrt(3) about 1.73 used; pushes forecasts to extremes.
limits: Coefficient tuned on their data; overfitting risk.
agent_relevance: Add a post-hoc extremize step as a calibration guardrail.

source: Aitchison et al. (2026) Diversity is the Strength of the AI Crowd
finding: Ensemble gains come from model diversity, not more samples from the best model.
numbers: Metaculus AI Benchmark Q2 2025 binary questions; budget B=5 best allocation splits across fine-tuned gpt-oss-120b, Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5, Grok 4. Grok 4 least replaceable despite third in solo accuracy.
limits: One tournament; short ICML 2026 workshop paper.
agent_relevance: Diversify reasoners instead of resampling one.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Advancing Event Forecasting through Massive Training of LLMs
finding: Review: LLMs gradually reaching superforecaster level; early claims had flaws.
numbers: Recaps GPT-4o 0.133, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.122, superforecasters 0.096, public 0.121; R1-14B 0.214 to 0.197 after RL. Flags small samples, questions resolved before cutoff, search contamination.
limits: Position paper, no new measurements.
agent_relevance: Confirms evidence base and caveats in this folder.

source: FRI ForecastBench leaderboard (task claim, not verified)
finding: Task text states gap to superforecasters 0.017 Brier (about one year of LLM progress) and parity near November 2026, wide interval.
numbers: Not verified. Leaderboard tables did not load; page says humans last surveyed July 2024 and models appear after a 50-day delay.
limits: Human baseline is old (July 2024); gap sensitive to question mix and crowd inputs.
agent_relevance: Treat 0.017 and Nov 2026 as unconfirmed until the live tables are read.
